stem: Which type of land tenure gives private ownership proved by a **title deed**?

stem: Under the Lancaster House constitution, how could the government obtain land for resettlement in the 1980s?

options.content: By seizing any farm without payment
options.rationale: Property was protected.

options.content: By order of the chiefs in each district
options.rationale: Chiefs had no such power.

options.content: By a vote of the United Nations
options.rationale: The UN had no role in this.

options.content: By buying it from willing sellers
options.rationale: Correct: willing-buyer willing-seller for ten years.

explanation: The willing-buyer willing-seller rule applied for ten years after independence.

stem: Nyasha wants to borrow money from a bank using her land as security. Which type of tenure would make this **easiest**?

State **four** aims of land reform in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Correct the colonial imbalance in land ownership
Decongest communal areas
Give land to the landless (including war veterans, women, youth)
Increase production / create black commercial farmers / fulfil a goal of the liberation struggle

stem: Explain **two** differences between communal land and freehold land.

points.description: Ownership: communal land is held for the community; freehold is privately owned
Developed: communal plots are allocated by traditional leaders and the RDC; freehold is proved by a title deed
Sale and security: communal land cannot be sold; freehold can be sold or inherited
Developed: freehold can be used as security for a loan; communal land cannot

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Communal land is held for the community and allocated to families by traditional leaders and the RDC, while freehold land is privately owned and proved by a title deed. Communal land cannot be sold, so it cannot be used as security for a loan, while freehold land can be sold, inherited or used to borrow money.

hints: Who owns it, and what can be done with it?

stem: Suggest **three** ways in which the government could help new farmers on resettlement land to increase production, explaining how each would help.

points.description: Secure tenure documents (e.g. bankable leases)
Developed: farmers can borrow and invest with confidence
Inputs and credit schemes
Developed: seed, fertiliser and equipment at planting time
Training and extension services / irrigation / markets
Developed: better skills, water and prices raise yields and incomes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The government could give farmers secure, bankable tenure documents, so they can borrow money and invest with confidence. It could provide inputs and credit schemes so that seed, fertiliser and equipment arrive in time for planting. It could expand training by extension officers and repair irrigation schemes, so that farmers use better methods and produce even in dry years.

hints: Think about tenure, inputs and skills.

stem: Answer the questions on land redistribution.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Outline the measures taken to redistribute land in Zimbabwe since 1980.

points.description: Willing-buyer willing-seller in the 1980s
Land Acquisition Act (1992): compulsory acquisition with compensation
Fast-track land reform from 2000 (A1 and A2 models)
Chapter 16 of the 2013 Constitution: acquired land vested in the State

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In the 1980s land was bought from willing sellers. The Land Acquisition Act of 1992 allowed compulsory acquisition with compensation. From 2000 the fast-track programme acquired most large commercial farms and allocated them under the A1 and A2 models. The 2013 Constitution, in Chapter 16, vests acquired agricultural land in the State.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "The willing-buyer willing-seller approach was a better way to redistribute land than fast-track land reform." Discuss.

points.description: For willing-buyer: orderly, legal, compensated; protected production and farm workers' jobs; kept investor confidence
Against willing-buyer: slow and expensive; land offered was often poorer; imbalance largely remained after twenty years
Fast-track: redistributed much land quickly to many families, but disrupted output and jobs and left tenure insecure
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Supporters of the willing-buyer willing-seller approach point out that it was orderly and legal: owners were paid, production continued and farm workers kept their jobs, and investors stayed confident.

However, it was slow and expensive. Government could buy only land that owners chose to sell, often of lower quality, and after twenty years the colonial imbalance largely remained.

Fast-track land reform redistributed a great deal of land to many families in a short time and addressed the historic injustice. But it disrupted commercial agriculture, many farm workers lost their jobs, and many new farmers lack secure tenure.

In my judgement neither approach was fully successful: willing-buyer willing-seller was fair to owners but did not achieve redistribution, while fast-track achieved redistribution at a high economic cost. A planned, faster but orderly approach with support for new farmers might have achieved more.

explanation: Outlining and comparing approaches to land reform.
hints: Judge each approach by speed, fairness and production.
